To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dollar-denominated borrowing is used by larger firms that are more exposed to foreign markets, that it is associated with lower investment in periods of exchange rate depreciation, and that these effects are stronger when the debt is long term.

dollar denominated borrowing by firms increases the likelihood of default, but also reduces the cost of borrowing in periods of high exchange rate volatility, and that these two effects are non-linear in the magnitude of exchange rate movements.

1) dollar-denominated debt in Chilean rms' balance sheet is associated with a negative balance-sheet eect; 2) this eect is more pronounced when the exchange rate depreciates strongly; 3) this eect appears to be non linear in the amount of the depreciation; and 4) the negative balance-sheet e ect is more pronounced for long term debt.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how firms' balance sheets are affected by exchange rate fluctuations and the role of debt contracts in determining these balance sheet effects.
the determinants of dollarization of firms' liabilities and the consequences for the balance sheet of exchange rate movements.
the causes and consequences for rms of the use of foreign currency denominated debt.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dollar denominated loans are a source of risk and that they should not be used as a way to hedge exchange rate risk.
the dollarization of debt contracts has not been a major problem for the Chilean economy.

the Chilean firms' balance sheet is not dollarized, but that there is a small group of firms which have dollarized their balance sheet, and that this group of firms has a negative response to exchange rate movements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dollar-denominated debts in Chilean firms are used to hedge the exchange rate risk and to reduce the cost of capital.
the use of dollar debt by Chilean firms appears to have increased the volatility of the real exchange rate, and has also reduced investment in periods of exchange rate depreciation.
the use of foreign currency debt is a rational choice for Chilean firms, but the negative balance-sheet effect of exchange rate movements can be large enough to reduce the investment of firms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of foreign currency denominated debt is a source of vulnerability that should be taken into account in the design of monetary policy.
the use of foreign currency debt is a rational response by firms to exchange rate volatility.
the balance-sheet channel is an important mechanism through which foreign currency debt can have real effects.
